The introduction lists green coffee, green tea and cinnamon as prior thermogenesis leads. The study administered neither of those ingredients as its intervention and did not measure Parkinson fatigue.
Black pepper, ginger and cinnamon appear in background references. Early abdominal pain was reported in the red chili extract group.
The Results record four participants with abdominal pain in the higher-dose extract group. The closing discussion's summary conflicts with that event count. No intensity estimate was reported.

Twenty-five healthy volunteers performed a manual Stroop task. Isolated inhaled eugenol had no detected reaction-time effect in the odor-versus-air comparison. The study did not assign clove ingestion.

Basil, paprika, anise seed and clove were among the 24 odor cues used across all rats. The assigned treatments were receptor antagonists and controls. The experiment did not compare any individual culinary exposure for executive function.
Celery seed was one of 24 odor cues. The study did not compare ingested celery leaves or clinical executive impairment.

Allspice and nutmeg served as sensory cues. Depression refers to synaptic long-term depression in the discussion. The experiment measured odor span, with no assigned spice intake or depressive symptom assessment.
Topical capsaicin deliberately provoked localized hand pain. Mean pain was 3.5/10 just before training, while the no-pain group reported none. The clinical ground cayenne comparison remains open.
